rv.q: The comedy-drama has been buffed to a scintillating sheen by director Scott Ellis and his lineup of pro designers.

With an impeccable cast headed by Jesse Williams, Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Patrick J. Adams, Take Me Out just might be a revelation even to those who saw the original Broadway production nearly 20 years ago.
Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Jesse Williams anchor a strong ensemble in Richard Greenberg's Tony-winning play about homophobia in professional baseball.
If the point of Take Me Out is to make us uncomfortable - to make us think, to force us to feel - then it's more than done its job. In fact, it's hit a home run.
I believe that that will be your takeaway from when you go to see it and I urge you that you should as it is a wonderful piece of theater.
Take Me Out impresses again with its wit, wisdom, and lyrical appreciation of baseball.
This convincingly-acted, blistering drama more than earns its championship title.

What’s truly impressive is the number, variety and depth of variations on the theme of personal identity that the author manages to coherently weave into his tale, most of which are successfully realized in Scott Ellis’ revival at the Theater under the aegis of Second Stage.
Scott Ellis’ production for Second Stage gets the maximum energy out of its shocking story.
Ferguson's performance is the real reason to see 'Take Me Out.'
Nonetheless, “Take Me Out” proves to be the highlight of the current theatrical season, thanks to Greenberg, Ellis and a uniformly superb cast who consistently hit it out of the proverbial park.
Under the uneven direction of Scott Ellis, Take Me Out becomes a cluster of both remarkable and insignificant performances pieced together inside a scattered plot.
Suavely performed, this new production doesn’t add all that much substance to the conversation.
The latter is a silly sitcom about trivial stereotypes.
In mapping the existential gap between player and team, between person and tribe, Take Me Out was ahead of its time — and still is.

cn.t: Critics praise this beautifully acted revival of Greenberg's Tony-winning play for its wit, rich writing, and timely exploration of identity, though some find it slow-burning and disjointed. The locker room drama remains relevant 20 years on.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
